claims.statement: dcode configuration is layered across user, project, session, and runtime scopes so teams can share project defaults while individual users keep their own credentials, preferences, skills, and local settings.

Configuration tiers are realized as ranked providers where lower numeric ranks win: managed policy (200), CLI arguments (300), retained runtime-reload values (350), environment (400), user config.toml (500), and manifest defaults (1000).

Managed policy is the strongest tier and the trust root; resolver_from_snapshots is keyword-only so a positional transposition cannot load the writable user file at the managed rank and grant user data managed precedence.

Configuration files are read into a single process-wide generation built on first read and reused after, and readers that resolve through the shared resolver all observe that one generation and cannot disagree about a setting.

The parsed command line is installed as a distinct CliProvider snapshotting the argparse namespace, and installing a different CLI provider for the same process is rejected because one argv yields one CLI tier.

The app does not watch configuration files for edits; an edit to config.toml while running has no effect on shared-resolver readers until the generation advances, because a partly applied configuration is treated as a worse failure than a stale one.
The shared generation advances in two places: an in-app write to the default config path, which refreshes the generation, and /reload.

Each configuration source keeps its last usable snapshot, so a file that fails to parse leaves that tier unchanged instead of erasing it; on reload the managed snapshot is refreshed in place rather than invalidated first to avoid presenting an empty managed table as 'no policy'.

A user config.toml that fails to parse on reload keeps the previous generation in force and is surfaced to the user with a 'Kept previous config.toml' notice, and a managed reload that cannot be enforced is surfaced as a blocking notice.

An in-app refresh fetches the managed snapshot before taking the resolver's generation lock and installs it as an already-refreshed replacement so policy installed since startup is picked up without blocking on remote I/O and without letting the user tier advance past the managed tier into a split-generation state.

Readers that step outside the shared generation are per-caller exceptions, not per-setting: a caller decides to snapshot a file itself, and no option is intended to be live for one reader and cached for another.

resolve_read_project_dotenv parses config locally on each call because it runs before the project .env is layered into the environment and needs a trusted-global-dotenv tier the shared resolver cannot express, avoiding establishing the process generation as a dotenv-bootstrap side effect.
The /reload preview reads the user config.toml fresh so the dry run shows the edit under review, and it deliberately does not refresh managed policy the process is enforcing.

The environment tier has no cached value: EnvProvider reads active_environment at resolution time, which is live os.environ outside construction and the construction-scoped immutable mapping inside use_environment; it is non-durable.

A managed policy candidate must be enforceable before it replaces the served policy generation, preventing an unreadable or invalid policy refresh from dropping restrictions and letting lower-ranked user configuration win.

Runtime reload installs a non-durable retained override provider at rank 350 only for accepted reloadable resolver values that the refreshed resolver cannot reproduce; the provider atomically replaces its retained value mapping.

The launcher serializes CLI-derived ServerConfig as DEEPAGENTS_CODE_SERVER variables; the server reconstructs it for graph assembly, and execution-time graph selection verifies the persisted thread workspace binding against the current non-secret policy and configuration fingerprint before building or reusing its workspace runtime.
ServerConfig clears environment variables for None values, normalizes CLI-derived relative paths before the subprocess boundary, and fails closed for malformed or unsafe filesystem-tool allowlists.

The server builds each workspace runtime against a dotenv-derived immutable environment and credential snapshot created off the server event loop; use_environment makes resolver reads during construction use that workspace snapshot rather than mutable process os.environ.

Project dotenv loading fills only absent environment values and denies repository-controlled values that would alter user-level MCP authorization, Auto review controls, subagent inheritance, graph recursion fallback, or launch terminal tracing; trusted shell and global dotenv inputs remain eligible.

Environment lookup helpers can give a DEEPAGENTS_CODE_-prefixed credential or provider variable precedence over its canonical name, including treating an explicitly empty prefixed variable as suppression of the canonical value.

The resolver enforces unique provider ranks and supports replace, union, and deep_merge strategies; union and deep_merge combine valid tier contributions rather than treating manifest defaults as normal accumulated values.
Workspace runtime caching is bounded to 32 bindings and keyed by each binding resource key; a configured sandbox is process-wide and rejects a second workspace claim.
